title: Faking Your Own Death: We All Do It, But Why?
summary: Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro voice) explore faking one's own death, or "pseudocide": why people do it (financial trouble, insurance fraud, escaping prison or abuse, lottery winners escaping relatives), how the Philippines became a hub for false death documents and bodies, how identity, cash, pets, microchips and digital traces lead to getting caught, and how insurance investigators pick up red flags. They cover case examples including Petra Pazzika, Sam Israel III, John Stonehouse, Marcus Schrinker, Curtis Wallin, and online death hoaxes such as Casey Nicole and Susan Meetze Mitchen. The episode closes with a discussion of faked online deaths tied to attention-seeking and factitious disorder, followed by a listener letter about Carnegie libraries' custodian apartments in New York City.

segments.title: Opening banter and definition of pseudocide
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about Jerry's absence and define pseudocide as faking your own death, noting that known cases are likely only the ones that were caught.

segments.title: Motives for faking death
segments.summary: Reasons people fake their death include financial debt, insurance fraud, embezzlement, facing long prison terms, escaping abusive relationships, and lottery winners avoiding relatives. Men and finance workers may be overrepresented, largely due to selection bias. Foreigners sometimes collect US insurance and return home.

segments.title: Elizabeth Greenwood and her book Playing Dead
segments.summary: The hosts credit Elizabeth Greenwood's book Playing Dead (2016) as an exhaustive look at pseudocide. She researched the process herself without going through with it and found the Philippines to be a hub for the service.

segments.title: Philippines fake documents and service tiers
segments.summary: Fake death certificates from the Philippines can reportedly be obtained for a couple hundred dollars. Higher-priced packages offer new identity kits, staged witnesses, and access to bodies.

segments.title: Black market bodies and cremains
segments.summary: Unclaimed bodies can be sold for pseudocide, as in the Philippines and an undertaker case in Coffee County, Georgia. The hosts discuss why cremated remains are used, and that some operators stage fake funerals with paid mourners. Legitimate funeral homes may also be exploited.

segments.title: Surveillance and getting caught by planning mistakes
segments.summary: Modern DNA, facial recognition, and cameras make evasion harder. Planning should start years ahead, building credit history. Staying in touch with former life, cash withdrawals, and pets with microchips are common pitfalls.

segments.title: Curtis Wallin's alter ego and cash and bitcoin trail
segments.summary: Artist Curtis Wallin created an alter ego in 2010 with a driver's license, tribal ID, boat license, and insurance, and merged his face with others to defeat facial recognition. The hosts discuss cash purchases, bitcoin being traceable on the public blockchain, and not draining bank accounts before disappearing.

segments.title: Legal exposure and police versus insurance investigators
segments.summary: Faking a death involves forgery and identity fraud even when no one is directly harmed. Police may not prioritize cases, but insurance investigators are more likely to pursue them. Hosts mention Magnum P.I. and Miami Vice in passing.

segments.title: Red flags that trigger insurance investigations
segments.summary: Insurers investigate large payouts (over a million dollars), sudden or suspicious deaths, inconsistencies in documents, deaths abroad, PO box mailing addresses, multiple policies applied for at once, and unusual medication purchases or visits to relatives. Mistakes include staying in the same city, online traces, and choosing a new identity too similar to the old one.

segments.title: Notable real cases: Petra Pazzika, Sam Israel III
segments.summary: Petra Pazzika, a German student who vanished in 1984 and was declared dead around 1989, was caught decades later when police checked her ID after a burglary; no charges were filed. Hedge fund manager Sam Israel III staged a suicide in 2008 by jumping from a bridge and was caught after calling his mother.

segments.title: John Stonehouse and Marcus Schrinker cases
segments.summary: UK MP John Stonehouse faked a drowning in Miami in 1974, fled to Australia with his secretary, and was caught after questions about a passport; the hosts note he followed steps from The Day of the Jackal. Marcus Schrinker staged a plane crash in 2009 after hiding cash in Alabama, parachuting out and emailing a friend afterward.

segments.title: Faked online deaths and factitious disorder
segments.summary: Faked online deaths tied to attention-seeking, as in the Casey Nicole leukemia hoax (2001) by Debbie Swinson, and romance author Susan Meetze Mitchen's fake suicide hoax in 2020. Other people faked deaths online to avoid obligations like knitting patterns or fan fiction. Factitious disorder and Munchausen syndrome are discussed.

segments.title: Listener mail: Carnegie libraries
segments.summary: Listener Madeleine Lovegrove, a children's librarian at the 125th Street New York Public Library, writes about Andrew Carnegie-funded libraries in New York City from 1901 that included custodian apartments, some still intact and some converted.
